note: How yeast/fermentation is handled, by archetype rather than per style. Every guideline category maps to one of these. Under this project's sourcing rule, a NUMERIC figure (pitch/inoculation rate) is committed only when cited to world-class professional documentation (primary/secondary: research institutes, industry bodies, peer-reviewed literature, manufacturer handbooks); blogs and retailer sites are never cited. An archetype whose primary figure is not yet retrieved carries researchStatus 'pending' and no number — described, not invented. Beer pitch-rate MATH lives in app/lib/pitching (White & Zainasheff); these records describe approach and point there.

archetypes.label: Ale — clean cultured yeast
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ale)
archetypes.approach: A measured pitch of a single clean ale strain at ale temperatures. Pitch rate follows the beer model in the pitching calculator (cells/mL/°Plato).
specialHandling: Standard ~0.75 M cells/mL/°P target for ales — see the pitching calculator.

archetypes.label: Lager — cold, high pitch
organisms: Saccharomyces pastorianus (lager)
archetypes.approach: Roughly double the ale pitch, fermented cold. The higher rate and low temperature keep esters down for a clean profile.
specialHandling: ~1.5 M cells/mL/°P; cold fermentation; diacetyl rest — see the pitching calculator.

archetypes.label: Belgian / saison — warm, ester-forward
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Belgian/saison, POF+)
archetypes.approach: Deliberately expressive: warmer fermentation (and sometimes a lower pitch) to encourage the esters and phenols that define Belgian ales and saison.
specialHandling: Under-pitching and free-rising warm ferments raise ester/phenol production — the opposite goal to a clean lager.

archetypes.label: Weissbier — banana & clove
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Weissbier, POF+)
archetypes.approach: A POF-positive wheat-beer strain fermented warm; pitch rate and temperature are tuned to balance isoamyl-acetate (banana) against 4-vinyl-guaiacol (clove).
specialHandling: Lower pitch / warmer = more banana; higher pitch / cooler = more clove.

archetypes.label: Mixed-culture / kettle sour
organisms: Saccharomyces
Brettanomyces
Lactobacillus
Pediococcus
archetypes.approach: A deliberate blend (or sequential pitch) of yeast and souring bacteria — pitched, not spontaneous. Flanders reds/browns, American wild, and kettle sours sit here.
specialHandling: Souring bacteria added alongside or before Saccharomyces; long maturation for Brett character.

archetypes.label: Spontaneous (lambic / coolship)
organisms: Enterobacteriaceae (Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Hafnia alvei) in the first month
Pediococcus damnosus with Saccharomyces cerevisiae and S. pastorianus from ~2 months
Dekkera (Brettanomyces) bruxellensis dominant from ~6 months, coexisting with P. damnosus
archetypes.approach: No yeast is pitched. Cooled overnight in an open coolship, the wort is inoculated by ambient microbiota and matures in barrels over 1–3 years.

standard.metric: microbial succession, not a pitch rate
standard.note: Spitaels et al. (2014), from >2000 isolates over two years at a traditional Belgian lambic brewery: no yeast is pitched; ambient coolship inoculation drives a reproducible succession (Enterobacteriaceae → Pediococcus damnosus + Saccharomyces → Dekkera bruxellensis) over a 1–3 year maturation.

specialHandling: No pitch: hot wort cools overnight in an open coolship and is inoculated by the ambient microbiota of the Senne valley.
Characteristic succession — Enterobacteriaceae (first ~3–40 days) → Pediococcus damnosus + Saccharomyces (~2 months) → Dekkera bruxellensis (~6 months onward).
Matures in barrels 1–3 years before bottling; seasonal (cool months), with no controllable pitch rate.

archetypes.label: Traditional opaque grain beer
organisms: Lactic acid bacteria: Limosilactobacillus (Lactobacillus) fermentum, Pediococcus acidilactici, Lactococcus lactis, Leuconostoc spp.
Yeast: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (dominant, 45–99% of the alcoholic phase)
archetypes.approach: African sorghum/millet opaque beers and European farmhouse grain ferments: sour, low-alcohol, often back-slopped from a previous batch rather than pitched from a pure culture. Drunk actively fermenting.

standard.metric: two-stage spontaneous fermentation, not a pitch rate
standard.note: Sawadogo-Lingani et al. (2021, dolo): a lactic-acid souring of the wort (12–16 h; LAB to 8.8–9.9 log CFU/mL, pH ~3.0–3.8) is followed by an alcoholic fermentation (9–14 h) on indigenous Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Seeded by back-slopping — part of a previous batch, or a sun-dried yeast leaven — rather than a measured pitch.

specialHandling: Two stages: spontaneous lactic souring first, then alcoholic fermentation on indigenous yeast.
Back-slopping seeds the next batch — a portion of previous beer or a sun-dried yeast leaven acts as the local starter.
Drunk while actively fermenting; sour and low in alcohol.

archetypes.label: Wine — active dry yeast, dosed by weight
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine)
archetypes.approach: Winemakers dose active dry wine yeast by weight per volume of must — a different standard from beer's cells/mL/°Plato. The yeast is rehydrated warm before inoculation.

standard.metric: g active dry wine yeast per hectolitre of must
standard.note: AWRI: an inoculum of 0.25 g/L (25 g/hL) to achieve a minimum 5×10^6 viable cells/mL; rehydrate in 5–10× the yeast weight of 38–40 °C water, stand 10–15 min. Up to ~2× for highly clarified, high-Brix, or high-SO2 musts.

specialHandling: Rehydrate warm; a rehydration nutrient (inactivated yeast) improves survival in difficult musts.
Higher dose for clarified/high-Brix/high-SO2 juice.
archetypes.comparison: Where beer counts cells/mL/°Plato, wine doses grams/hL — the same idea (enough viable cells) expressed in the winemaker's units.

archetypes.label: Wine — native / spontaneous
organisms: indigenous non-Saccharomyces (Hanseniaspora, Metschnikowia, …) giving way to Saccharomyces cerevisiae
archetypes.approach: No yeast added; the must ferments on the vineyard/winery microbiota. A per-style choice within many wine categories rather than a separate legal class.
specialHandling: Higher risk and variability; the non-Saccharomyces early phase shapes aroma before Saccharomyces finishes.

archetypes.label: Biologically-aged (flor) wine
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae flor strains (film-forming)
archetypes.approach: Fino/manzanilla sherry: after fermentation a film (flor) of specialised yeast grows on the wine surface under a solera, ageing it oxidatively-protected.
specialHandling: Flor film forms at specific alcohol (~15%) and requires the solera system.

archetypes.label: Sparkling — second fermentation (tirage)
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (bayanus/prise-de-mousse type)
archetypes.approach: A base wine is re-fermented with added sugar and a robust yeast (liqueur de tirage) in bottle or tank to trap CO2; the classic method ages on lees.
specialHandling: Alcohol-tolerant, flocculent yeast for the second ferment; lees ageing for autolytic character.

archetypes.label: Fortified — fermentation arrested by spirit
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine)
archetypes.approach: Port-type wines: a normal wine ferment is stopped early by adding grape spirit, killing the yeast and leaving residual sweetness at a higher strength.
specialHandling: Fermentation is deliberately halted mid-way; timing of the spirit addition sets sweetness.

archetypes.label: Cider — cultured wine/cider yeast
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine/cider active dry yeast)
archetypes.approach: Modern cider often pitches a cultured wine or cider yeast, frequently after sulphiting the juice to suppress wild flora — closer to the wine model than the beer one.

standard.metric: g active dry yeast per hectolitre of juice
standard.note: Scott Laboratories: 2 lb/1000 gal (25 g/hL) for a standard primary fermentation, rising to 2.8 lb/1000 gal (35 g/hL) for high-Brix juice above 25 °Bx. The same dose-by-weight standard as wine — AWRI gives 25 g/hL for a minimum 5×10⁶ viable cells/mL — so the inoculation calculator's g/hL model applies directly.

specialHandling: Dosed by weight per volume like wine, not by cells/mL/°Plato like beer.
Nutrient-poor apple juice benefits from yeast nutrient; cool, slow ferments preserve aroma.
Juice is commonly sulphited before pitching to suppress the wild flora the cultured yeast is meant to outcompete.

archetypes.label: Cider — wild / keeved (traditional)
organisms: indigenous yeast and bacteria of the fruit and cellar
archetypes.approach: Traditional French/Basque/English ciders ferment on wild flora; keeving deliberately starves the ferment (via a pectin gel, the chapeau brun) to leave natural sweetness. No pitch.

standard.metric: nutrient depletion by keeving; no pitch rate
standard.note: Januszek et al. (2024): keeving (défécation) adds calcium chloride and pectin methylesterase to the must. Demethylation of the homogalacturonan chain in pectin lets it bind calcium and form a gel, which CO₂ floats to the surface as the chapeau brun over roughly 2–6 days. Around 50% of the pectin and nutrients are trapped in that cap and the sediment beneath it; the resulting shortage of assimilable nitrogen makes the fermentation slow and stop of its own accord, leaving residual sweetness.

specialHandling: Keeving starves rather than stops: nutrient removal, not sulphite or filtration, is what arrests the ferment.
Calcium chloride plus pectin methylesterase drive gel formation; the chapeau brun rises within about 2–6 days.
Slow and low-temperature by design — the point is an incomplete fermentation with natural sweetness left in.

archetypes.label: Mead — wine yeast + staggered nutrients
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine)
archetypes.approach: Honey is nutrient-free, so mead pitches a wine yeast and manages fermentation through staggered nutrient additions rather than pitch rate alone. The builder computes a TOSNA-style schedule (lib/must.ts).
specialHandling: Staggered nutrient additions (TOSNA) over the first third of fermentation; without them, sluggish ferments and H2S.

archetypes.label: Sake — kōji + sake yeast (multiple parallel fermentation)
organisms: Aspergillus oryzae (kōji, saccharification)
Saccharomyces cerevisiae — kyōkai sake yeast (kōbo, fermentation)
archetypes.approach: A common misconception is that kōji ferments the sake. It does not: kōji mould saccharifies the rice (amylase/protease), while a SEPARATE sake yeast — usually a kyōkai strain from the Brewing Society of Japan, added via the shubo/moto starter — carries out the alcoholic fermentation. Both run at once in the moromi, 'multiple parallel fermentation', with rice, water and kōji added in three stages (sandan-jikomi).
specialHandling: Shubo/moto starter built first (sokujō fast-souring, or kimoto/yamahai slow lactic).
Kōji and yeast work simultaneously in the main mash.
archetypes.comparison: Unlike beer (mash then pitch) or wine (crush then pitch), saccharification and fermentation happen together, which lets sake reach unusually high alcohol.

archetypes.label: Huangjiu (Chinese yellow wine) — qū starter
organisms: Moulds of the qū: Aspergillus oryzae, Rhizopus oryzae, Mucor spp., Monascus purpureus
Yeast: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (the principal ethanol producer)
Bacteria: Lactobacillus spp., Bacillus spp., Weissella, Leuconostoc
archetypes.approach: Chinese yellow rice wine uses a qū starter — a cake of grain colonised by a consortium of moulds, yeasts and bacteria — to saccharify and ferment together, related to but distinct from Japanese kōji.

standard.metric: semi-solid open fermentation; no pitch rate
standard.note: Tian et al. (2022): wheat qū supplies the amylase, protease and esterase that saccharify the starch while Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments the released sugars — simultaneous saccharification and alcoholic fermentation, termed semi-solid open fermentation. A typical course runs ~30 °C for 5–7 days, after which the mash is opened to drop to ~15 °C and held 1–2 months to finish.

specialHandling: Qū supplies both saccharifying enzymes and fermenting organisms.
Saccharification and alcoholic fermentation run simultaneously (semi-solid open fermentation), not in sequence.
Lactic acid bacteria dominate the bacterial community, and which species dominate tracks with product quality.

archetypes.label: Korean rice wine — nuruk starter
organisms: Moulds of the nuruk: Aspergillus, Rhizopus and Mucor spp.
Yeasts: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (>90% of the fungal community through fermentation) and Saccharomycopsis fibuligera
Lactic acid bacteria: Lactilactobacillus curvatus, Liquorilactobacillus satsumensis, Pediococcus acidilactici
archetypes.approach: Takju/makgeolli and yakju use nuruk, a traditional grain fermentation starter carrying both saccharifying moulds and yeast.

standard.note: Song et al. (2022): nuruk is made by natural solid fermentation of moistened ground rice or wheat, growing a mixed population of moulds, yeasts and lactic acid bacteria. Its moulds release amylase and glucoamylase to saccharify the rice while the yeasts ferment the released sugars. The gayangju course they followed ran ~25 °C for the fermentation stages, then ~15 °C for an aging period of about 35 days.

specialHandling: Nuruk carries both the saccharifying moulds and the fermenting yeasts — there is no separate yeast pitch in the traditional method.
Lactic acid bacteria persist throughout and shape the finished acidity.
Often a multi-stage build (a first and second fermentation) before an extended cool aging.

archetypes.label: Southeast Asian rice ferment — ragi / starter cake
organisms: Amylolytic moulds: Amylomyces rouxii (some isolates reclassified as Mucor indicus), Rhizopus oryzae, Mucor spp.
Yeasts: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Candida utilis, Endomycopsis burtonii
Lactic acid bacteria: Pediococcus pentosaceus, Lactobacillus plantarum, L. fermentum
archetypes.approach: Tapai and related SE-Asian rice ferments use ragi — a dried starter cake of amylolytic mould plus yeast — inoculated onto cooked rice.

standard.note: Delva et al. (2022): ragi tapai is a dry starter cake (~2.5 cm across, ~0.5 cm thick) of rice flour, spices and a mixed microbial culture. Amylomyces rouxii is the principal amylolytic organism, producing amyloglucosidase and growing on raw substrate. Two functional groups do the work — one breaks starch down to glucose, the other converts glucose to ethanol.

specialHandling: The starter is a physical cake crumbled over cooked rice, not a liquid pitch.
Two functional groups: amylolytic moulds saccharify the starch, yeasts ferment the glucose.
Related starters across the region go by different names — chu (China), ragi (Indonesia), ragi-tapai (Malaysia), bubod (Philippines), marcha (India), nuruk (Korea).

archetypes.label: Whisky wash — congener-developing distiller's yeast
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (distiller's / M-type; sometimes with brewer's yeast)
archetypes.approach: The wash is fermented for flavour, not clean neutrality: distillers pick strains and conditions that develop esters and higher alcohols (congeners), which carry through distillation into the spirit's character.
specialHandling: Warmer / more-stressed ferments and congener-forward strains raise esters; cooler, cleaner ferments reduce them.

archetypes.label: Rum wash — osmophilic yeast + dunder
organisms: osmophilic Saccharomyces; dunder/muck microbiota for heavy styles
archetypes.approach: Cane/molasses washes use osmophilic yeast; heavy 'high-ester' rums recycle dunder (stillage) in muck pits to build the acids and esters that define the style.
specialHandling: Dunder/muck concentrates esters and acids; long, warm, deliberately funky ferments.

archetypes.label: Neutral spirit wash — low-congener yeast
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (low-congener / vodka-type)
archetypes.approach: Vodka, gin base and neutral spirit want the opposite of whisky: a low-metabolite yeast and clean conditions that minimise congeners for a neutral distillate. Higher fermentation temperature tends to lower esters and raise higher alcohols.
specialHandling: Low-congener strain; controlled temperature to minimise flavour compounds.

archetypes.label: Brandy — wine base, then distil
organisms: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (wine)
archetypes.approach: Grape and fruit brandies ferment as wine first (wine yeast, wine handling) and are then distilled; the fermentation archetype is the wine one, with distillation added.
specialHandling: Follow the wine-cultured approach; low-SO2 base wine for distillation.

archetypes.label: Agave spirits — cultured or wild
organisms: cultured Saccharomyces, or autochthonous wild yeast (traditional mezcal)
archetypes.approach: Cooked-agave musts are fermented either with a cultured yeast (industrial tequila) or on wild/ambient flora in open wooden vats (traditional mezcal), which drives much of the rustic character.
specialHandling: Open-air wild ferments for traditional styles; strain choice for industrial.

archetypes.label: Baijiu — Daqu/Xiaoqu, solid-state fermentation
organisms: complex Daqu/Xiaoqu microbial consortium (moulds, yeasts, bacteria)
archetypes.approach: Baijiu is made by solid-state fermentation of grain with a qū starter (Daqu or Xiaoqu) — a self-sustaining microbial consortium — often in earthen pits, then solid-state distilled. Not a single pitched yeast.
specialHandling: Solid-state, pit/vessel-dependent microbiota; aroma type (香型) follows the qū and process.

archetypes.label: Distilled milk liquor (arkhi)
organisms: kefir-type lactose-fermenting yeast + lactic acid bacteria
archetypes.approach: Central Asian milk liquor distils fermented mare's/cow's milk (airag/kumis): the lactose is fermented by a kefir-type yeast-and-bacteria culture, then distilled.
specialHandling: Back-slopped milk culture; lactose (not maltose/sucrose) is the sugar.

archetypes.label: Regional traditional spirits
organisms: varies by tradition (wild or local starter)
archetypes.approach: Feni, palm distillates and other regional spirits ferment on local wild flora or a regional starter before distillation; handled per style rather than one rule.
specialHandling: Map per style as primary sources are secured.

archetypes.label: Spontaneous sap/juice ferment (palm wine, pulque, chicha)
organisms: wild Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Zymomonas mobilis, plus non-Saccharomyces yeasts and lactic acid bacteria
archetypes.approach: Palm sap (palm wine), agave sap (pulque) and maize (chicha) ferment spontaneously on the microbes already present in the sap and environment — no yeast is added. In palm wine, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Zymomonas mobilis are the main alcohol producers.
specialHandling: Very fast (hours to a day); the microbial mix shifts continuously and drives the flavour.
Traditionally drunk fresh, still fermenting.

archetypes.label: Fermented milk (airag / kumis / kefir)
organisms: symbiotic lactic acid bacteria + lactose-fermenting yeast (kefir-type)
archetypes.approach: Mildly alcoholic fermented milks are back-slopped from a living culture of lactic bacteria and yeast that ferment lactose — a starter culture, not a pitched pure strain.
specialHandling: Back-slopping maintains the culture; simultaneous souring and light alcohol.

archetypes.label: SCOBY ferment (kombucha)
organisms: symbiotic culture of acetic acid bacteria and yeast (SCOBY)
archetypes.approach: Kombucha ferments sweetened tea with a SCOBY — a symbiotic pellicle of acetic-acid bacteria and yeast added from a previous batch (with starter liquid), not a measured yeast pitch.
specialHandling: Low alcohol; the bacteria oxidise ethanol to acid, giving the sour profile.

archetypes.label: Wild / back-slopped grain & folk ferments
organisms: wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria
archetypes.approach: Kvass, tesgüino and other folk grain ferments run on wild flora, often back-slopped, and are drunk young and lightly alcoholic. Handled per tradition.
specialHandling: Back-slopping; short, low-alcohol ferments.

archetypes.label: No yeast added (pruno)
organisms: whatever is present — wild and from added bread; uncontrolled
archetypes.approach: Improvised prison wine adds no cultured yeast; fermentation relies on wild organisms and any bread thrown in. It is included as a warning, not a method: pruno has caused documented botulism outbreaks.
specialHandling: No pitch, no control; genuine public-health hazard — see the pruno guideline entry.
